title: Ticket Triage: Sorting and Routing with AI

thumbnail.headline: Sort Tickets, Protect Customers
thumbnail.image: Navy background, a stream of ticket cards splitting into coloured lanes, one red card marked with a shield going into a fast lane, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Sort Tickets, Protect Customers
slide.body: Ticket cards flowing into four coloured lanes; one red card with a shield icon jumps to a fast lane. Small tag: AI for Customer Experience and Support · Lesson 5.

production_notes: [VERSION] Free-plan access and data-use terms of Claude and ChatGPT must be checked before recording.
Katarzyna and the Polish digital bank are fictional; stock footage must show no real bank names, cards or logos.
The worked example uses old tickets with all personal details removed; the exercise uses made-up tickets only.
The content says the AI and the senior agents 'agree on most tickets but not all'; no agreement percentage is given, and none should be added to slides.

Hook.voiceover: A customer writes: my card was used in another country, and I did not make these payments. If that message waits behind fifty password questions, the customer may lose more money. Sorting tickets well is not only about speed. Sometimes it is about safety.

Explain.voiceover: Welcome to week two. This week we design AI-assisted workflows, and we start with ticket triage. Triage means reading each new message, deciding what kind it is, and sending it to the right place.

slide.title: Ticket Triage: Sorting and Routing with AI
slide.body: AI for Customer Experience and Support · Lesson 5 of 12 · Week 2

Explain.voiceover: AI can do the first step by adding labels. The common ones are topic, such as billing or delivery. Urgency, such as high, normal or low. Language, so the right agent can read it. And sentiment, the customer's mood. Then a routing rule sends the ticket on. For example, card fraud goes to the fraud team with high priority.

slide.title: Label, then route
slide.body: New ticket → four tags: Topic · Urgency · Language · Sentiment → routing rule: 'Topic = card fraud → Fraud team, high priority'.

Explain.voiceover: How does AI choose a label? A language model compares the meaning of the message with the category names and descriptions you give it. It does not only look for keywords, so it understands that the courier never came is a delivery problem. But it is still a prediction, and predictions can be wrong, even when they sound confident.

slide.title: Meaning, not only keywords
slide.body: Message: 'The courier never came' → label: Delivery (no keyword 'delivery' in the text). Small warning: it is still a prediction.

Explain.voiceover: A wrong label has a real cost. A fraud report labelled as a billing question may wait for days. A calm message from a vulnerable customer may be marked low urgency.
Explain.stock_query: worried person looking at bank card and phone
Explain.on_screen_text: A wrong label has a cost

Explain.voiceover: So two things matter. First, clear categories. Each one needs a short description and one or two examples, and categories must not overlap. If payments and billing both exist, and nobody can explain the difference, the AI will not know either. Second, checking the results. Compare AI labels with labels from experienced agents, and keep checking a sample after launch.

slide.title: Two things that matter
slide.body: 1. Clear categories: short description · one or two examples · no overlap. 2. Check results: compare with experienced agents · keep checking a sample after launch.

Explain.voiceover: A useful extra rule is an unsure category. Tell the AI: if the message does not clearly fit one category, label it needs review. A person sorts these by hand. That is better than a confident wrong label.

slide.title: The 'Needs review' rule
slide.body:
If the message does not clearly fit one category,
label it "Needs review".

Explain.voiceover: Think of a sorting desk at a big post office. Most letters have clear addresses and go straight to the right van. A good sorter puts the hard-to-read ones in a box for a supervisor, instead of guessing.
Explain.stock_query: postal worker sorting letters into boxes
Explain.on_screen_text: Unsure? Put it aside for a person.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Here is an example. Katarzyna leads support at a hypothetical digital bank in Poland. Customers write in Polish, English and Ukrainian. Her team uses five categories: card and fraud, payments and transfers, account access, loans, and other.
Demonstrate.stock_query: support team lead at desk in european office

Demonstrate.voiceover: She writes a short description for each. Card and fraud means lost or stolen cards, payments the customer did not make, and suspicious messages that ask for codes. Every card and fraud ticket is high priority, and any ticket the AI is unsure about goes to needs review.

slide.title: Category description
slide.body:
Card and fraud: lost or stolen cards, payments the customer did not make, suspicious messages that ask for codes.
Rule: always high priority.
Unsure → Needs review.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Before launch, she takes sixty old tickets, with all personal details removed. Two senior agents label them, and then the AI labels the same tickets. They agree on most, but not all.

slide.title: Test before launch
slide.body: 60 old tickets (personal details removed) → two columns: Senior agents' labels | AI labels → compare. Most rows green, a few amber.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Katarzyna studies the differences. The AI labelled, someone called me pretending to be from the bank, as account access, not fraud. So she adds phone calls from people pretending to be the bank to the fraud description. She tests again, and the results improve. A senior agent now checks a small sample every week.

slide.title: Fixing the description
slide.body: Before: 'Someone called me pretending to be from the bank' → Account access (red). Fix: add 'phone calls from people pretending to be the bank'. After: → Card and fraud (green). Weekly sample check.

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to test once and stop checking. A new product, a new scam or an outage brings new kinds of messages. The categories that worked last month may not fit this month. Keep checking samples, and update your descriptions.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, AI triage labels tickets by topic, urgency, language and sentiment, so routing rules can send them to the right team. Second, clear categories with short descriptions and a needs review option reduce wrong labels. Third, compare AI labels with human labels before launch, and check a sample regularly after launch.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Labels: topic, urgency, language, sentiment → routing. 2. Clear categories + 'Needs review'. 3. Compare with human labels before launch; check samples after.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise, you will define five categories, write fifteen made-up tickets, and label them yourself. Then an AI assistant labels them too, and you count the differences. In the next lesson, we map the workflow and decide what to automate, what to assist, and what stays human. See you there.
